children: Brent crude futures topped $100/bbl on Wednesday for the first time since July 24 as ​escalating attacks in the Middle East, including on tankers, heightened concerns about energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
The move brought futures prices into line with physical crude ‌and fuel markets, where prices have already been trading above the psychological threshold.

The oil price rally accelerated this week after multiple attacks on Saudi oil installations by Iran-backed Houthi militants increased the risk that disruptions could spread across the wider Persian Gulf region; U.S. forces have since hit multiple Iranian oil tankers and ⁠Iran targeted a U.S. base in Jordan and attacked ships.

A tanker carrying 2M barrels of Iraqi fuel oil was struck by a drone in ​Iraqi territorial waters on Wednesday, port officials said, and several merchant vessels in the Gulf reportedly were hit by disabling fire overnight.

"Recent developments only reinforce the view that we’re still some way from a restart in talks," and the absence of a credible path back to negotiations is likely to keep a sizable geopolitical risk premium in prices, ING analysts Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey said in a note.

The oil market had coped better than initially expected because of inventories, alternative export routes, and shifts in Chinese buying, but that resilience is becoming a growing market risk as inventories are being depleted, Rystad Energy chief economist Claudio Galimberti said.

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has "come down massively" during the recent escalation of hostilities, from ~8M bbl/day during the last week of August to only 1M bbl/day this week, according to Rystad.

"The key risk is whether the recent attacks on oil tankers lead to fewer ship-to-ship transfers taking place in the Gulf of Oman, ​which have so far played a key role in providing oil to global markets and keeping a lid on prices," according to Hamad Hussain of Capital Economics.
